title: Implement soil fertility and plant nutrition practices

lessons.title: Interpreting soil and leaf analyses
lessons.html:
From data to decisions

Implementing a nutrition programme at NQF level 4 means understanding the analysis reports, working with the adviser's recommendations and making sure they are applied correctly and their effects tracked.

Reading a soil analysis report

  • pH (water or KCl): indicates acidity; KCl values are typically lower than water values. Compare with the crop's target range given by the lab or adviser.
  • Exchangeable acidity and acid saturation: high acid saturation indicates aluminium toxicity risk and the need for lime.
  • Phosphorus: reported by a specific extraction method (e.g. Bray 1 or Olsen); interpretation depends on the method used.
  • Exchangeable cations (K, Ca, Mg, Na): and their ratios; high sodium indicates sodicity and structural problems.
  • CEC (cation exchange capacity): the soil's capacity to hold nutrients; sandy soils have low CEC and need smaller, more frequent applications.
  • Organic carbon: indicates organic matter levels.
  • Micronutrients: such as zinc and boron.
  • Texture (clay percentage): affects lime requirement and nutrient behaviour.

Leaf and tissue analysis

Leaf analysis shows what the plant has actually taken up. Samples must be taken at the specified growth stage and leaf position, as norms are only valid for that sampling protocol. Leaf analysis is especially valuable in orchards, vineyards and long-season crops.

Nutrient budgets

Advisers often use a nutrient balance: crop removal for the yield target, plus corrections for soil deficiencies, minus contributions from soil reserves, manure and previous crops such as legumes. This approach avoids over-application that wastes money and pollutes water, and under-application that limits yield.

Diagnosing problems in the field

Combine visual symptoms, soil and leaf results, irrigation records and history. Rule out root problems, waterlogging, compaction, nematodes, herbicide damage and disease before concluding a deficiency.

lessons.title: Implementing and monitoring the nutrition programme
lessons.html:
Turning the recommendation into a programme

Translate the recommendation into a block-by-block schedule:

BlockProductRate (kg/ha)TimingMethod
Land 3Dolomitic limePer recommendationPre-plant, incorporatedSpreader
Land 3Compound fertiliserPer recommendationAt plantingBanded with planter
Land 3LANPer recommendationTop-dress at the specified growth stageSpreader

Order products in time, check deliveries against the order and product analysis, and store them correctly.

Calibration

  • Calibrate spreaders and planters for each product, because density and granule size differ.
  • Check spread pattern and bout width to avoid striping.
  • For fertigation, calibrate injectors, check EC and pH of the nutrient solution and flush the system after injection.

Organic sources

Manure and compost vary widely in nutrient content; have them analysed where possible and include their contribution in the budget. Apply raw manure with care near harvest of fresh produce because of food safety risks; follow the farm's food safety rules.

Safety and environment

  • Wear PPE as indicated on product labels; dust masks and gloves for powders, eye protection for liquids and acids.
  • Store ammonium nitrate-based fertilisers away from fuels and combustibles.
  • Avoid application near watercourses, on saturated soils or before heavy rain.
  • Use only registered fertilisers (Act 36 of 1947).

Monitoring

  • Record every application: date, block, product, rate, method and operator.
  • Scout crops for symptoms; take leaf samples at the specified stage.
  • Compare yield and quality per block with nutrient applied.
  • Repeat soil analysis at regular intervals to track pH and nutrient trends.

Reviewing

At season end, review results with the adviser and adjust the next programme. Calculate fertiliser cost per tonne produced to assess economic efficiency.

Key points

  • Understand pH, acid saturation, P method, cations, CEC and organic carbon on reports.
  • Leaf samples must follow the correct stage and leaf position.
  • Build schedules per block with product, rate, timing and method.
  • Calibrate equipment for each product.
  • Record applications, monitor crop response and review yearly.
